name: Royal Prussia
info: A province of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland, formed from Teutonic Order lands in 1466, self-governing until 1569 and annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia in the partitions of Poland.

facts.capital: No single capital; the great cities Danzig (Gdańsk), Thorn (Toruń) and Elbing (Elbląg) led the province
facts.founder: Created by the Second Peace of Thorn (1466) after the Prussian Confederation's revolt against the Teutonic Order
facts.successor: Kingdom of Prussia (province of West Prussia)

t: Royal Prussia was formed when the Prussian Confederation of nobles and burghers rose against the Teutonic Order in 1454 and the Thirteen Years' War ended with the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466.
Until 1569 it kept its own laws, council and parliament, and only Prussians could hold its offices under the ius indigenatus.
The Union of Lublin of 1569 integrated it fully into the Kingdom of Poland, and the partitions of 1772 and 1793 gave its lands to the Kingdom of Prussia.
dyk: Before the Union of Lublin, the Polish chancellor openly admitted that integrating Royal Prussia breached the law by violating the privileges granted in 1454.
ev: Nobles and cities found the Prussian Confederation at Marienwerder against the Teutonic Order's policies
King Casimir IV Jagiellon issues the Incorporation Act, and the Thirteen Years' War begins
The Second Peace of Thorn cedes Pomerelia and western Prussia to the Polish Crown
After the priests' war, Warmia is formally incorporated into Poland
The Statute of Prussia brings many Polish legal solutions into the Prussian legal system
Sejmiks are established and the Prussian parliament takes its bicameral form; Protestantism becomes the ruling religion in Danzig, Elbing and Thorn
The Union of Lublin integrates Royal Prussia fully into the Kingdom of Poland
In the first partition of Poland the Kingdom of Prussia annexes most of the former Royal Prussia

sections.foundation:
Pomerelia, originally Polish, became a fully independent duchy in 1227 and was seized by the Teutonic Knights in 1309, after Władysław I the Elbow-high had asked them for help against Brandenburg. Papal courts in 1320 and 1339 ordered its return to Poland. Under the Order the burden of taxation and arbitrary rule bred resistance: the Chełmno Land nobility founded the Lizard League in 1397, and after the Battle of Grunwald in 1410 and the heavy compensation of the 1411 Peace of Thorn, nobles and burghers met in a joint assembly in 1412. In 1440 they founded the Prussian Confederation at Marienwerder (Kwidzyn), led by the citizens of Danzig, Elbing and Thorn.

In February 1454 the Confederation sent a delegation under Jan Bażyński to King Casimir IV Jagiellon, declaring him the only true sovereign of their lands. On 6 March 1454 the Royal Chancellery issued the Incorporation Act, which accepted the Prussians as subjects, incorporated Prussia into the Polish kingdom and granted considerable autonomy. The war that followed ended in October 1466 with the Second Peace of Thorn.
sections.socioeconomy:
The province took in Pomerelia with the mouth of the Vistula and the city of Danzig, the Chełmno and Michałów Lands with Thorn, the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia with Frauenburg, Heilsberg and Allenstein, and the Marienburger Land with Marienburg and the city of Elbing. At the start of the 15th century the Order's lands held a mixed population: about 200,000 Germans, 140,000 native Prussians and about 140,000 Poles; Poles were two thirds of Pomerelia's people and half of the Chełmno Land's. About 110,000 people, nearly a quarter of the population, lived in 93 towns.

Trade was central to the province's privileges. The Prussian estates were exempted from the Pfundzoll and guaranteed freedom of trade, and Thorn and Danzig kept the right to mint coins. In 1529 a monetary union joined Royal Prussia, Ducal Prussia and the rest of the kingdom. Kulm law guaranteed inheritance also in the female line, which led to the fragmentation of estates; in 1522 the nobility demanded the Polish model of inheritance and land ownership.
sections.military:
Royal Prussia was born of war. After the Prussian Confederation pledged allegiance to Casimir IV on 6 March 1454, the Thirteen Years' War, the War of the Cities, began; the king appointed Hans von Baysen (Jan Bażyński) war-time governor and took oaths from the citizens of Toruń, Elbląg and Königsberg. The war also drew in cities of the Order's eastern lands such as Kneiphof. The Knights won the Battle of Chojnice in 1454 but could not pay for enough knights to retake the castles held by the insurgents, and thirteen years of attrition ended with the Second Peace of Thorn in October 1466.

Later conflicts were smaller. A short war, the so-called priests' war, settled the claim of the bishop of Warmia to independence in the king's favour in 1479. In 1498 Frederick of Saxony, elected Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, pursued a hostile policy to reclaim lost territories. In the Order's last war against Poland, in 1519–1521, Albrecht von Hohenzollern was defeated, and the Polish General Assembly met at Toruń in 1519 and at Bydgoszcz in 1520.
sections.governance:
Royal Prussia kept its existing law codes and borders, and only Prussians could be appointed to its offices (ius indigenatus). It was divided into voivodeships on the Polish model: after 1466 Pomeranian, Chełmno and Marienburg (Malbork). By a decision of the Polish Sejm in 1467 its main governing body was the Prussian council (Landesrat): three voivodes, three castellans, three chamberlains and two delegates from each of Thorn, Danzig and Elbing, later joined by the bishops of Warmia (1479) and Chełmno (1482), 17 members in all. From 1508 the bishop of Warmia headed it. Because the council could not tax without the commons, an assembly of the estates grew into a bicameral Prussian parliament in 1512–1526.

The kings governed through a governor, an office abolished in 1467, then a starosta general from 1472, which Stibor von Baysen refused in protest. Nicolaus von Baysen led the opposition from 1485 against violations of the ius indigenatus. The Statute of Prussia of 1506, a central treasury and a supreme tribunal of 1511 brought the province closer to the kingdom; Danzig decided its cases internally.
sections.impact:
The province was the meeting ground of Polish and Prussian political cultures. Its estates stood for deep particularism, sent only token delegations to the royal elections of 1492, 1501 and 1506, and yet were drawn step by step into the kingdom: Lucas Watzenrode took part in a Senate meeting in 1509 as the first representative of the Prussian council, summons to the Sejm went to the Prussian sejmiks from 1537, and in 1548 both Prussian chambers sent deputies and senators to the Sejm. Closer ties found support above all among the ordinary nobility, who found Polish political and legal solutions more favourable.

The Reformation also crossed into Royal Prussia. After the Order's state was secularised as the Duchy of Prussia under the Lutheran Albrecht, Lutheranism spread especially in the big cities, and Protestantism was declared the ruling religion in Danzig, Elbing and Thorn after 1526, though part of their population remained Catholic. Albrecht had Luther's Catechism translated into Old Prussian, Polish and Lithuanian to unite the people of both Prussias, while the Polish king tried to stop the spread of Protestantism.
sections.decline:
Royal Prussia's autonomy ended in 1569 with the Union of Lublin, which created the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. The province was integrated fully into the Kingdom of Poland, its parliament was reduced to a provincial assembly and incorporated into the Sejm of the Commonwealth, and its other separate institutions were dissolved. Before the union was concluded, the Polish chancellor openly admitted that the act breached the law by violating the privileges granted in 1454.

Its lands were thereafter governed as the Pomeranian, Chełmno and Malbork Voivodeships and the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia. Across the border, the Duchy of Prussia passed in 1618 into personal union with the Electorate of Brandenburg and in 1657, by the Treaty of Wehlau, gained full independence, allowing its later elevation to a kingdom. In the first and second partitions of Poland, in 1772 and 1793, the Kingdom of Prussia, the successor state of the Teutonic Order, annexed the former territory of Royal Prussia and reorganised it as the province of West Prussia.

summary: Royal Prussia was the western half of the Teutonic Order's Prussia, which its nobles and burghers took into the Kingdom of Poland in 1454 and won in the Thirteen Years' War. Self-governing under its own council and parliament until the Union of Lublin of 1569, it was annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia in the partitions of 1772 and 1793.
references: Friedrich, Karin, The Other Prussia: Royal Prussia, Poland and Liberty, 1569–1772 (Cambridge University Press, 2000)
Frost, Robert, The Making of the Polish-Lithuanian Union 1385–1569 (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Dwyer, Philip G., ed., The Rise of Prussia 1700-1830 (Routledge, 2000)
Odyniec, Wacław, Dzieje Prus Królewskich (1454–1772). Zarys monograficzny (Warszawa, 1972)

pointDescs.1466: The Second Peace of Thorn ends the Thirteen Years' War and cedes Pomerelia and western Prussia to the Polish Crown.
pointDescs.1467: The Sejm makes the Prussian council the province's main governing body.
pointDescs.1479: After the priests' war Warmia is incorporated, and its bishop joins the Prussian council.
pointDescs.1506: The Statute of Prussia is promulgated; a central treasury and in 1511 a supreme tribunal follow.
pointDescs.1526: Sejmiks are established and the bicameral Prussian parliament takes shape.
pointDescs.1548: Both Prussian chambers send deputies and senators to the Sejm for the first time.
pointDescs.1569: The Union of Lublin integrates the province fully into the Kingdom of Poland and dissolves its separate institutions.
pointDescs.1657: The Treaty of Wehlau gives neighbouring Ducal Prussia full independence.
pointDescs.1772: The first partition of Poland gives the former Royal Prussia to the Kingdom of Prussia.

notes: The article names no capital; I gave the three leading cities instead. 'Federal' tag is a loose fit for a self-governing province. The power curve is the province's autonomy and standing rather than power: it is a province, not a sovereign state. The article ends the Prussian annexation in 1772 and 1793 (Danzig and Thorn presumably in 1793, but the article does not say which parts when), so I did not split it. Population figures are for the Teutonic lands c. 1400, as the article gives them.
